RAGPULSE, we reveal RAG-specific system
bottlenecks that are obscured by generic LLM
traces and synthetic RAG datasets, including

design and evaluation in real-world RAG work-
loads, our work enables more specialized, data-

ticularly for long-context inference and memory-
efficient serving (Zheng et al., 2026).
2
Preliminary and Motivation
2.1
Why We Need a Real-World RAG Trace
with Temporal Information?
Existing generic LLM-Specific traces are funda-
mentally inadequate for RAG serving systems.
This limitation arises from the distinctive workload
characteristics of RAG, which diverge substantially
from standalone LLM inference and thus require
dedicated, RAG-specific traces.
First, RAG introduces an inherent multi-stage
execution pipeline. Each request traverses mul-
tiple tightly coupled phases—including retrieval,
re-ranking, and generation (Yu et al., 2025; Asai
et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024). End-to-end latency, re-
source utilization, and cache behavior are therefore
governed by cross-stage interactions rather than by
generation alone. Generic LLM traces, which pri-
marily capture the prefilling and decoding phase,
fail to expose these composite system effects.
Second, RAG performance is highly depen-
dent on both the underlying knowledge base and
real-world query patterns (Yue et al., 2025; He
et al., 2024; Gutiérrez et al., 2024). Workload
dynamics such as query similarity and document
cache hit rates vary significantly with user behav-
ior. Moreover, practical deployments often exhibit
strong inter-request correlations, where consecu-
tive queries share overlapping contexts or retrieved
documents. Accurately capturing these temporal
and content-level dependencies is essential for op-
timizing scheduling, batching, and KV cache reuse
policies (Agarwal et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2024).
Third, most existing RAG traces are derived
from synthetic or curated chat workloads, which
typically contain limited document corpora and
lack authentic temporal locality information. Op-
timizations validated on non-representative traces
often fail to generalize to production environments,
resulting in performance gaps and unstable system
behavior. This disconnect substantially hinders the
practical advancement of RAG serving systems.
Beyond characterization, RAG-specific traces
are critical for enabling joint optimization of re-
trieval and generation. Treating these components
as independent black boxes limits the design space
of RAG serving systems. In contrast, realistic RAG
traces make it possible to co-optimize retrieval
caching, query-adaptive batching, and scheduling
decisions across pipeline stages (Wang et al., 2024).
Taken together, these limitations underscore the
need for a real-world, production-grade RAG trace
to ground system design and evaluation in realistic
workload behaviors.

level analyses and optimizations that are otherwise

Dataset Usage and Applications
To validate the effectiveness of proposed RAG-
PULSE dataset for evaluating system performance
in real-world environments, we have constructed
a dedicated benchmarking platform. This section
provides a detailed description of this platform’s
specific implementation, the composition and us-
age methodology of the dataset, and the perfor-
mance evaluation metrics employed.
5.1
Implementation
We constructed a prototype system for an online
RAG service to simulate real-world applications.
The system’s core is built upon vLLM (v0.10.1)
and LMCache (v0.3.1) (Kwon et al., 2023; Cheng
et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2025a), a
widely adopted open-source inference framework.
To emulate a typical RAG workflow, the system
integrates an end-to-end pipeline, encompassing
user request reception, text processing, and final
result generation. All experiments are conducted
on a server equipped with a single NVIDIA A100
GPU with 80GB VRAM. We deploy Qwen3-8B as
the generator component of RAG pipeline.
5.2
Scaling RAGPULSE to Any Scale
RAGPULSE’s trace data is characterized by a sig-
nificant temporal span. This property provides re-
searchers with high flexibility, allowing them to
slice or scale the trace data according to specific
experimental goals. For example, a high-traffic pe-
riod (e.g., one hour) can be isolated to benchmark
the system’s peak concurrent processing capabili-
ties. Conversely, the entire long-term trace can be
used to assess the long-term efficacy of caching
policies, such as the KV cache management. More-
over, an analysis of throughput fluctuations in the
trace enables a deeper comprehension of the sys-
tem’s behavioral patterns under varying loads.
5.3
Performance Metrics
We evaluate the RAG serving system using two
standard LLM-serving metrics that capture perfor-
mance across prefill and decoding phases: (1) Time
to First Token (TTFT), measuring end-to-end la-
tency from request arrival to the first generated
token and reflecting user-perceived responsiveness;
and (2) Time Per Output Token (TPOT), measur-
ing the average latency of subsequent tokens and
reflecting generation throughput. This distinction
is vital as prefill is compute-bound, whereas decod-
ing performance is primarily limited by memory
bandwidth (Agrawal et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2025).

The RAGPULSE benchmark employs a client-
server architecture for workload replay.

streaming and non-streaming modes to capture
key metrics such as TTFT and TPOT. An asyn-
chronous, concurrent design ensures stability and
high throughput under heavy load.
The client acts as the load generator. Its three-
stage workflow includes: (1) preprocessing the
trace file; (2) dispatching requests strictly adher-

scaling factor to adjust replay speed; and (3) record-
ing performance metrics for subsequent analysis.

8
Conclusion
RAG has emerged as the standard paradigm for
building trustworthy, high-performance LLM appli-
cations. However, its unique retrieval architecture
introduces unprecedented challenges for system
optimization. Existing generic LLM traces and
synthetic RAG datasets fail to capture RAG spe-
cific workload dynamics, creating a significant gap
between academic research and deployment.
To bridge this gap, we introduce RAGPULSE,
an open-source RAG workload trace dataset that
preserves authentic temporal information missing
in existing traces. Through in depth analysis, we
reveal critical characteristics of production RAG
workloads including time sensitive document reuse
and bursty temporal locality. These findings pro-
vide empirical grounding for next generation RAG
optimizations such as temporal aware scheduling
and semantic aware caching, establishing a stan-
dard for efficient RAG serving.
Limitations
Although RAGPULSE captures authentic temporal
reuse patterns, several aspects remain unexplored.
First, while the trace includes multi turn conversa-
tions, it does not yet capture more complex agentic
workflows such as tool use or iterative retrieval
generation cycles across multiple reasoning steps.
Second, the trace includes only text based docu-
ments, and multimodal RAG scenarios involving
images or audio are not covered. Finally, to pro-
tect user privacy, we release RAGPULSE as an
encrypted, privacy-preserving trace. Although this
does not affect RAG system optimization, it re-
moves raw semantic information. We will explore
incorporating richer semantic metadata through
privacy-preserving techniques (Feyisetan and Ka-
siviswanathan, 2021; Meehan et al., 2022) and con-
sider releasing original content after obtaining user
consent in future versions of RAGPULSE.
